title: Accidental Hypothermia — Staging & Rewarming
keywords: mild 35-32C, moderate 32-28C, severe 28-24C, profound under 24C, the Swiss staging system uses clinical signs to estimate the stage when a core temperature isn't available yet

summary: The Revised Swiss Staging System lets you estimate hypothermia severity from clinical signs alone when core temperature isn't yet available — mild stays shivering and alert, moderate loses shivering and consciousness dims, severe becomes unconscious with vital signs still present, profound looks like death but a hypothermic patient isn't dead until they're warm and dead.
whyThisMatters: Cold myocardium is electrically irritable and rough handling or premature defibrillation attempts in a severely hypothermic patient can precipitate the very arrhythmia you're trying to prevent, which is why gentle handling and modified resuscitation rules exist specifically for this population — and because a profoundly hypothermic patient can present looking clinically dead with fixed pupils and no detectable pulse yet still be neurologically salvageable after rewarming, the usual rules for declaring death don't straightforwardly apply.
clinicalTakeaway:
Stage clinically when core temperature isn't yet available:
- Mild (shivering, alert), roughly 35-32°C, gets passive external rewarming (warm environment, blankets, remove wet clothing).
- Moderate (shivering stops, consciousness impaired), roughly 32-28°C, gets active external rewarming (warm blankets/forced-air warming) plus careful monitoring.
- Severe (unconscious, vital signs present), roughly 28-24°C, and profound (may appear dead), below 24°C, need active core rewarming, gentle handling to avoid precipitating arrhythmia, and in cardiac arrest, consideration of ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass for rewarming alongside CPR.

Below 30°C, follow modified resuscitation guidance — space out or withhold defibrillation attempts and vasopressor dosing per current protocol, since a cold heart doesn't respond normally to either.

A hypothermic patient in arrest isn't declared dead until rewarmed (or until further resuscitation is deemed futile per protocol) — 'not dead until warm and dead.'

rows: Passive external rewarming — warm environment, insulation, remove wet clothing; the patient can often generate their own heat via shivering
Active external rewarming — warm blankets, forced-air warming devices — plus cardiac monitoring; loss of shivering means the patient can no longer self-rewarm
Active external AND core rewarming (warmed IV fluids, warmed humidified oxygen, body cavity lavage where available) with continuous cardiac monitoring given high arrhythmia risk
No, or minimal, vital signs — may appear clinically dead
Active core rewarming, CPR if in arrest, and consideration of extracorporeal rewarming (ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass) — 'not dead until warm and dead'

body.text: This system was specifically designed for use when an accurate core temperature ISN'T immediately available (a common field/prehospital situation) — clinical signs (consciousness, presence of shivering, vital signs) let you estimate the stage and guide initial management before a core temperature probe result comes back.
Gentle handling — a cold heart is electrically irritable

Handle a moderately-to-severely hypothermic patient GENTLY — rough movement, repositioning, or unnecessary jostling can precipitate ventricular fibrillation in a cold, irritable myocardium. This is not a routine trauma logroll/transfer situation; minimize movement and handle deliberately.

items: Below 30°C, a cold heart may not respond normally to defibrillation or vasopressors — current guidance generally supports limiting defibrillation attempts and spacing out (or withholding) vasopressor dosing until the core temperature rises above this threshold, rather than repeating standard-interval ACLS dosing on a hypothermic arrest.

Continue CPR while actively rewarming — a hypothermic arrest is treated as potentially reversible with rewarming in a way a normothermic arrest of the same duration would not be, which is the basis for the 'not dead until warm and dead' principle.

Extracorporeal rewarming (ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass) is the fastest and most effective rewarming method for a patient in cardiac arrest from severe/profound hypothermia, when available — it simultaneously provides circulatory support and core rewarming, and should be considered early rather than as a last resort in a center with that capability.
